lead: Montana water damage comes from frozen pipes, spring runoff and mountain floods. DryFlare helps owners from Billings to Missoula and Bozeman get homes dry.
risk: frozen pipes, spring snowmelt and river flooding, and ice jams
why: Montana's cold snaps can push temperatures far below zero. Pipes freeze in cabins, crawl spaces and second homes that sit empty for weeks. A pipe that splits in an empty cabin can run for days before anyone finds it.

Spring melt and rain-on-snow cause floods. In June 2022, the Yellowstone River and its creeks flooded Red Lodge, Gardiner and Livingston. Ice jams on the Missouri and Yellowstone can also push water into towns in late winter. Wyoming and Idaho share these mountain risks.
image_alt: Close-up of stacked sandbags for flood protection
image_caption: Rain on fast-melting snow can flood Montana's river towns in a single day.
problems: Yellowstone, Clark Fork and Missouri river towns
Homes in Bozeman, Whitefish and mountain towns
tips: Winterize cabins by draining the lines or keeping heat at 55°F or higher.
Install a smart leak sensor and auto shut-off in second homes.
Clear snow from roofs and away from foundations before spring.
Check FEMA flood maps if you live near a river.
insurance: Many Montana policies limit freeze claims in unheated or vacant homes, so read the terms for cabins and seasonal homes.

faq.q: How do I protect a Montana cabin from frozen pipes?
faq.a: Drain the plumbing and water heater when you close it for winter, or keep heat on at 55°F or higher. A remote temperature sensor can alert you if the heat fails. Shut off the main water valve when you leave.

licensing: Contractors with employees must register with the Montana Department of Labor and Industry. Plumbers and electricians need state licenses, and some cities add local rules.
